title: Adaptive Contracts for Cost-Effective AI Delegation
claim: An abstract two-party interaction proceeds step by step, with a selective second-stage evaluation, and maps directly onto a concrete AI application.
layout: 2 columns zigzag top-to-bottom, boxes with arrows, dual-color abstract/application text
description: Two columns of boxes, Principal on the left and Agent on the right, joined by arrows that zigzag downward to show the order of interaction. The principal first commits to an adaptive contract (p, s, t). The agent takes a best-response action and incurs a cost. The principal then observes a coarse signal k, and if p_k = 1 pays to inspect it and sees an outcome j. The agent receives payment s_k or t_{k,j}. The principal finally receives reward r_{k,j}. Each box has black text with math notation for the abstract setting. Below it is a parenthetical italic line, blue for the principal and orange for the agent, giving the LLM-delegation meaning. The eye goes first to the bold role headers, then follows the arrows down.
caption: Principal-agent interaction in an abstract adaptive contract setting. Colored text describes the application to AI task delegation.
abstract: When organizations delegate text generation tasks to AI providers via pay-for-performance contracts, expected payments rise when evaluation is noisy. As evaluation methods become more elaborate, the economic benefits of decreased noise are often overshadowed by increased evaluation costs. In this work, we introduce adaptive contracts for AI delegation, which allow detailed evaluation to be performed selectively after observing an initial coarse signal in order to conserve resources. We make three sets of contributions: First, we provide efficient algorithms for computing optimal adaptive contracts under natural assumptions or when core problem dimensions are small, and prove hardness of approximation in the general unstructured case. We then formulate alternative models of randomized adaptive contracts and discuss their benefits and limitations. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the benefits of adaptivity over non-adaptive baselines using question-answering and code-generation datasets.
